passages.t: Husband and wife: each belongs to the other
passages.happening:
Here Paul turns to the letter the Corinthians had sent him. “Now for the matters you wrote about: It is good to abstain from sexual relations” (verse 1).

But Paul does not leave it there. “But because there is so much sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” (verse 2).

Then he speaks of sex within marriage, and he speaks of both partners in the same way. “The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (verse 3). “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (verse 4).

“Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control” (verse 5).

Paul says this is a concession, not a command (verse 6). He wishes everyone were as he is, unmarried. “But each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Who said ‘It is good to abstain from sexual relations’? The Berean Standard Bible prints it without quotation marks. But many translators and readers think Paul is quoting the Corinthians' own letter back to them, as he quoted their slogans in 6:12-13. If so, some in Corinth had swung to the opposite extreme from the men who went to prostitutes. They thought even married sex was unspiritual, and that holy people should give it up. Others take the words as Paul's own view of singleness, which he then limits. On either reading, Paul answers that married couples should not stop living as married people.

Now notice how verses 3 and 4 are built. Every line has a pair: husband and wife, wife and husband. In the Greek and Roman world that was not how marriage was usually spoken of. A husband's rights over his wife were taken for granted. Ancient writing on marriage rarely said that a wife has the same authority over her husband's body as he has over hers. And it was not counted a disgrace for a married man to visit a prostitute, so long as he did not overdo it. Paul says the husband belongs to his wife as fully as she belongs to him. In that world this was remarkable.

‘Marital duty’ means what each owes the other in marriage. Paul does not mean a debt one partner can demand from the other. He means a gift each gives, with neither keeping themselves from the other.

‘Mutual consent’ in verse 5 is a key phrase. Even a pause for prayer must be agreed by both, not decided by one.

‘Gift’ in verse 7 is the Greek charisma, the same word Paul uses for gifts of the Spirit in chapter 12. Readers take it in two ways: that marriage and singleness are each a gift from God, or that the gift in view is the self-control that makes singleness good for some.
passages.ot:
Paul's view of marriage rests on the first pages of the Bible. God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper” (Genesis 2:18), and the two “will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).

The Old Testament speaks warmly of love within marriage. Proverbs says, “may you rejoice in the wife of your youth” (Proverbs 5:18), and Ecclesiastes, “Enjoy life with your beloved wife” (Ecclesiastes 9:9). The Song of Songs gives the woman her own voice: “My beloved is mine and I am his” (Song of Solomon 2:16). The mutual belonging Paul describes is already there.

The law of Moses also protected a wife's rights in marriage. If a man took a second wife, “he must not reduce the food, clothing, or marital rights of his first wife” (Exodus 21:10).
passages.hard:
Do verses 3 to 5 give a husband, or a wife, the right to demand sex?

No. This must be said plainly, because these verses have been misused. Paul is saying that each partner belongs to the other, and that neither should hold back from the other. He is not giving anyone permission to force, pressure or threaten. The very same passage requires ‘mutual consent’. And the love Paul describes later in this letter is patient and kind, and “it is not self-seeking” (13:5).

Consent matters within marriage. A wedding does not give anyone ownership of another person's body in the sense of being able to take what is not freely given. Forcing or pressuring a husband or wife into sex is wrong, and it is abuse. These verses were written to set wives and husbands on equal ground, not to give one power over the other.

If you are being pressured or forced in your marriage, it is not your fault, and these verses do not ask you to submit to it. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul describes a marriage where each belongs to the other, freely and equally. If you are married, ask whether that describes how you treat your husband or wife: giving rather than taking, agreeing together rather than deciding alone. If you are not married, ask what this passage says about how God values the body and the bond between two people.

passages.happening:
“Now to the unmarried and widows I say this: It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am” (verse 8).

“But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Paul was unmarried when he wrote this. Whether he had been married before is not known; the letter does not say.

Roman society pushed people hard toward marriage. Laws of the emperor Augustus, passed in 18 BC and AD 9, penalised adults who stayed unmarried and rewarded those who had children. Widows and divorced women of child-bearing age were expected to marry again within a set time. Against that pressure, Paul's words that it is ‘good’ to remain single sounded very different.

In Jewish life too, marriage and children were expected of nearly everyone. Paul, a Jew, is saying something unusual: a single life can be good, and full, and given to God.

But Paul is not making singleness a rule. ‘If they cannot control themselves, let them marry.’ ‘Burn with passion’ means to be consumed by desire. Paul does not treat that as shameful. He treats marriage as the right and good answer to it.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament usually expects marriage. God's first word to the man and woman was, “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28). But it also makes room for those who do not marry. Through Isaiah God promised to the eunuchs who keep his covenant “a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5). God told the prophet Jeremiah, “You must not marry or have sons or daughters in this place” (Jeremiah 16:2), so even his single life became a message.

Jesus spoke of some who live unmarried “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12), and said that this was not for everyone: “Not everyone can accept this word” (Matthew 19:11).

And God is the protector of widows: “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5).
passages.hard:
A word to readers who are single. Some have chosen it for God's sake. Many did not choose it, or have not chosen it yet, or are single after loss or divorce. Some cannot marry for reasons they did not choose. This passage does not ask you to explain yourself. Paul, who was single, calls singleness ‘good’ and a gift. Jesus, who was single, spoke of it with honour. You are not unfinished, and you are not a problem to be solved. A church that treats single people as if they were has not listened to Paul or to Jesus.

And a word to widows and widowers. Paul gives you freedom here, not a rule: to remain as you are, or to marry. Either is good.
passages.asks: If you are single, ask what freedom your life holds now, and how you might give it to God and to others. If you are married, ask how you honour the single people around you, in what you say and in whom you make room for at your table. And ask whether your church speaks of singleness as Paul does, as a good gift, or as a waiting room.

passages.t: Divorce, and a believer married to an unbeliever
passages.happening:
Paul now passes on a command of Jesus. “To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband” (verse 10). “But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife” (verse 11).

Then he turns to a case Jesus had not spoken of: a believer married to an unbeliever. “To the rest I say this (I, not the Lord): If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her” (verse 12). The same holds for a believing wife (verse 13).

The reason: the unbelieving husband or wife is ‘sanctified’ through the believing partner. “Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (verse 14).

But there is another case. “But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called you to live in peace” (verse 15).

Paul ends with a question to each: “How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Paul is careful to say where each word comes from. In verse 10 he says ‘not I, but the Lord’: he is passing on what Jesus taught. In verse 12 he says ‘I, not the Lord’: Jesus had not spoken to this situation, so Paul gives his own ruling as an apostle. That is honest, and it helps readers. Paul does not put his own words into Jesus's mouth.

In Roman law either a husband or a wife could end a marriage, simply by leaving with the intention of ending it. There was no court and no paperwork. So to separate and to divorce were close to the same thing. That is why Paul uses the words ‘separate’ and ‘divorce’ side by side.

A mixed marriage, a believer married to an unbeliever, was common in Corinth. Often one partner had come to faith after the wedding. Some believers may have worried that staying married to a pagan would make them unclean. Paul says the opposite. The believer is not made unclean by the marriage. The unbelieving partner is ‘sanctified’, set within God's reach through the believer, and the children are ‘holy’. Paul does not mean the unbeliever or the children are saved without faith. He means the household is not defiled, and the marriage stands under God's claim.

Then the case of desertion. If the unbelieving partner leaves, the believer should let them go. The believer is ‘not bound’. The Greek word, douloō, means to be made a slave. The believer is not a slave to a marriage the other has walked out of. ‘God has called you to live in peace.’

Verse 16 can be read two ways. Some read it as hope: stay, because you may win your partner to faith. Others read it as a release: you cannot know that you will, so do not hold on to a marriage the other has left for the sake of saving them.
passages.ot:
Behind ‘not I, but the Lord’ stands the teaching of Jesus, which Paul agrees with and passes on. Jesus went back behind the law of divorce to the beginning, to Genesis 1:27 and Genesis 2:24: the two “will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). “Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate” (Mark 10:9). Mark gives Jesus's words without an exception (Mark 10:11-12). Matthew adds the words “except for sexual immorality” (Matthew 19:9). The notes on Mark 10 and Matthew 19 say more, and these notes agree with them.

The rule about divorce that Jesus answered is Deuteronomy 24:1-4. It assumes divorce happens and puts limits on it. Through the prophet Malachi God says of a husband and the wife of his youth, “the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant” (Malachi 2:14).

Paul's ruling on mixed marriages goes a different way from one moment in Israel's history. After the exile, Ezra led men who had married foreign wives to send them away (Ezra 10:3). Paul tells believers not to send away an unbelieving partner who is willing to stay.
passages.hard:
What does this passage allow about divorce and remarriage? This is one of the hardest questions in the letter. It touches many real lives, and Christians answer it in more than one way. Each answer is held by careful readers, and each is set out here as its holders would put it. These notes do not decide between them.

What Paul says is clear in outline. For two believers, he passes on Jesus's command: no divorce. If a wife does separate, she should stay unmarried or be reconciled (verse 11). For a believer married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay, the believer should not seek a divorce. If the unbeliever leaves, the believer is ‘not bound’ (verse 15). The question is what ‘not bound’ means.

Some hold that marriage cannot be dissolved while both live, so there is no divorce with remarriage at all. The Catholic Church teaches that a true sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved while both spouses live, though it allows separation and can declare that a true marriage never existed. Catholic canon law also reads verse 15 in its own way, called the Pauline privilege: when one of two unbaptized spouses is baptized and the other departs, the first marriage can be dissolved and the believer may marry again.

Some hold that divorce may happen but remarriage may not. On this view ‘not bound’ frees the believer from the duty to keep the marriage going, but not to marry someone else while the former spouse lives. Some scholars read Jesus's teaching in the same way.

Many hold that adultery and desertion free the innocent partner to remarry. This is the reading of most Protestant churches. They take Matthew's exception, ‘except for sexual immorality’ (Matthew 19:9), together with ‘not bound’ here. The Westminster Confession of 1646 names adultery and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied as the only grounds that dissolve the bond. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be for life but, as an act of mercy, allow a second marriage with a service of repentance.

Others hold that there are wider pastoral grounds. Many count abuse as breaking the marriage covenant, as surely as desertion. Some argue that the cases Jesus and Paul named show a principle that reaches other ways a marriage can be destroyed. Others answer that the Bible names only these grounds and no more.

What all of them share is Jesus's main point. God meant marriage to last for life, and divorce is always a tearing of what he joined. And all of them read Paul's ‘God has called you to live in peace’ as part of the answer.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. The site's Honest Answer, ‘What does the Bible say about divorce and remarriage?’, says more.
passages.asks: Paul treats marriage as worth keeping, even a hard one, and he also refuses to make a believer a slave to a marriage the other has left. Ask what it would mean in your life to honour both. If divorce has touched your life, by your choice or not, remember that Jesus spoke to defend the one with no power, and that God has called you to peace. You are not a second-class believer.

passages.t: ‘Remain in the situation you were in’: circumcision and slavery
passages.happening:
Paul gives a rule he teaches in every church. “Regardless, each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him. This is what I prescribe in all the churches” (verse 17).

He gives two examples. The first is circumcision. A man who was circumcised when called should not try to become uncircumcised, and a man who was uncircumcised should not be circumcised (verse 18). “Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commandments is what counts” (verse 19). “Each one should remain in the situation he was in when he was called” (verse 20).

The second is slavery. “Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let it concern you” (verse 21). Then: “if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity” (verse 21).

“For he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman. Conversely, he who was a free man when he was called is Christ’s slave” (verse 22). “You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men” (verse 23).

He repeats the rule a third time: each should remain with God in the situation he was in when called (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Paul's rule sits in the middle of his teaching on marriage, and it explains it. Coming to faith did not mean a believer had to change every part of their life to be acceptable to God. A married person did not need to leave a marriage. A single person did not need to marry. A Jew did not need to stop being a Jew, and a Gentile did not need to become one. God called each person where they were.

Circumcision was the mark of the covenant for Jewish men. Some Gentile believers felt pressure to be circumcised, to become more fully part of God's people. Paul says no. Circumcision is not what makes a person acceptable to God. ‘He should not become uncircumcised’ means a Jewish believer should not try to hide or undo the mark.

Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world. Slaves did almost every kind of work, from mines and fields to teaching and keeping accounts. One historian has estimated that slaves made up at least a tenth of the empire's whole population, and far more in some places. Many people in a city like Corinth were slaves or former slaves, and the church held both. But Roman slavery was often not for life. Masters often freed slaves, sometimes as a reward, sometimes in a will, sometimes because the slave had saved enough to buy freedom. So a slave in the church might really have a chance to become free.

Verse 22 turns the world's ranks upside down. The slave is ‘the Lord's freedman’, someone the Lord has set free. The free man is ‘Christ's slave’, owned by Christ. In the church, both stand on the same ground.

‘Do not become slaves of men’ (verse 23) is strong. Believers belong to Christ, who bought them. They must not hand themselves over to any other master.
passages.ot:
Circumcision was given to Abraham as the sign of God's covenant: “Every male among you must be circumcised” (Genesis 17:10). Paul does not despise it. He says that what counts is “Keeping God’s commandments” (verse 19). He says the same in other letters: “All that matters is faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6), and “What counts is a new creation” (Galatians 6:15).

Israel's God is the God who frees slaves. The commandments begin, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). The law said Israelites were God's servants and “are not to be sold as slaves” (Leviticus 25:42). It forbade kidnapping a person to sell (Exodus 21:16). And it said, “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you” (Deuteronomy 23:15).

‘Bought at a price’ (verse 23) repeats 6:20. Behind it lies God's rescue of Israel from slavery, and the price of Christ's death.
passages.hard:
What does Paul tell slaves to do in verse 21? The Greek of the second half of the verse is very short, and it can be read two ways. Scholars have long been divided.

The Berean Standard Bible reads, ‘if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity’. On this reading Paul says: do not let slavery trouble you as if it made you less before God, but if you can become free, do. Many translations read it this way.

Other translations take it the opposite way: even if you can become free, make the most of your present condition, that is, use it to serve God. Those who read it so point to the rule Paul repeats three times in this passage, ‘remain in the situation he was in’. Those who read it the first way answer that Paul's next words are ‘do not become slaves of men’ (verse 23), and that no one would tell a slave to turn down freedom. These notes do not choose between the translations.

Three things are plain on either reading. First, Paul says a slave's worth before God is not lessened at all: the slave is ‘the Lord's freedman’. Second, he tells believers not to give themselves to anyone as slaves (verse 23). Third, nothing in this verse tells anyone today to accept being held, owned or forced to work. The Bible itself counts the slave trade among sins, listing “slave traders” among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). Paul asked Philemon to receive his slave Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16).

Why did the New Testament not simply forbid slavery? The site's Honest Answer, ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’, faces that question.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul tells believers they do not have to change their station to be acceptable to God. Ask whether you have thought that God would accept you more if your circumstances were different. Then ask the other side: where do you have the freedom to change something unjust, for yourself or for someone else, and are you taking it?

passages.t: ‘The time is short’: virgins, and undivided devotion
passages.happening:
Paul takes up the next question. “Now about virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give a judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy” (verse 25).

“Because of the present crisis, I think it is good for a man to remain as he is” (verse 26). If you are committed to a wife, do not seek to be released. If you are free, do not look for a wife (verse 27). “But if you do marry, you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (verse 28). But married people will face troubles, and Paul would spare them.

“What I am saying, brothers, is that the time is short” (verse 29). Those with wives should live as if they had none; those who weep, as if they did not; those who rejoice, as if they did not; those who buy, as if they had nothing; those who use the world, as if not bound to it (verses 29-31). “For this world in its present form is passing away” (verse 31).

“I want you to be free from concern” (verse 32). The unmarried man or woman can be concerned with the Lord's work. The married person is also rightly concerned with pleasing a husband or wife, and so their interests are divided (verses 32-34). Paul says this for their good, “not to restrict you, but in order to promote proper decorum and undivided devotion to the Lord” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
‘Virgins’ here means young people, most likely young women, who had never married and were perhaps promised in marriage. In that world marriages were usually arranged by families.

Paul says plainly that he has no command from the Lord about this. He gives his own judgment, as one the Lord has made trustworthy. That tells readers how to take what follows: as wise advice from an apostle, not as a law. He says the same at the end of the chapter: “In my judgment” (verse 40).

What was ‘the present crisis’? Readers answer in different ways. Some think of a particular hardship pressing on Corinth at the time, such as a shortage of food. Others think of the troubles that mark the whole time between Christ's rising and his return, when believers live under pressure in a world that is passing away. Others think Paul expected the end very soon, and spoke with that in mind. Paul does not say exactly, and these notes do not decide.

‘The time is short’ means the time has been shortened, drawn together. Christ has come, and the end has begun. That changes how believers hold everything: marriage, grief, joy, possessions. Paul does not tell them to stop marrying, grieving, rejoicing or buying. He tells them not to be owned by any of it.

Verses 32 to 34 are about focus, not holiness. Paul does not say married people are less holy. He says, simply, that a husband or wife rightly cares about pleasing the other, and that takes time and thought. A single person may have more freedom to give undivided attention to the Lord's work.
passages.ot:
The world ‘passing away’ is a theme of Scripture. John writes, “The world is passing away, along with its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever” (1 John 2:17). Peter says, “The end of all things is near” (1 Peter 4:7). Paul himself writes in Romans, “our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed” (Romans 13:11).

Jesus spoke of the hardships of the last days, and of how hard they would be for families: “How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers” (Mark 13:17).

Paul's wish that believers be ‘free from concern’ echoes Jesus's words to Martha, who was busy with many tasks: “you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:41-42).
passages.hard:
Paul marks carefully which words are a command of the Lord and which are his own judgment (verses 10, 12, 25, 40). What does that tell us about how to read him?

It tells us that Paul knew the difference, and wanted his readers to know it too. He did not claim that every opinion he held was a word from Jesus. When he had a word from Jesus, he said so. When he did not, he gave his best judgment, as a trustworthy apostle who says, “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (verse 40).

Christians hold that all of Paul's letter is Scripture, given by God, including the parts where Paul gives his own judgment. But Paul himself shows that not every sentence carries the same kind of weight. Some are commands. Some are advice for a particular time, ‘because of the present crisis’, and Paul says so. Readers who take the Bible seriously have to read with the same care Paul wrote with.

So the advice not to marry was not a law, and Paul says plainly that those who marry ‘have not sinned’. Some churches through history held up a single life as more holy than marriage. Others have treated marriage as the only full life. Paul honours both.
passages.asks: Paul asks believers to hold everything loosely, because this world is passing away. Ask what you hold too tightly: a relationship, money, a plan, a grief. Ask what ‘undivided devotion to the Lord’ would look like in your present situation, married or single, and what distracts you most from it.

passages.happening:
Paul turns to a man and the young woman he is promised to. If he thinks he is not acting rightly toward her, and she is getting older and they ought to marry, “let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning; they should get married” (verse 36).

But if he is settled in his mind, under no pressure, and decides not to marry her, “he will do well” (verse 37). “So then, he who marries the virgin does well, but he who does not marry her does even better” (verse 38).

Last, widows. “A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord” (verse 39). In Paul's judgment she will be happier if she stays as she is. “And I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Verses 36 to 38 are among the hardest in the chapter to translate, and readers take them in three ways. Most modern translations, including the Berean Standard Bible, take them to describe an engaged man deciding whether to marry the woman he is promised to. An older reading, found in the King James Version, takes the man to be a father deciding whether to give his unmarried daughter in marriage. That fits the verb in verse 38, which can mean ‘give in marriage’. A third, less common view pictures a couple who had promised to live together without sex. On every reading, Paul's point is the same: marrying is not sin, and not marrying for the Lord's sake is also good.

‘Does even better’ in verse 38 must be read with the whole chapter. Paul has just said, twice, that those who marry do not sin. ‘Better’ is about freedom for the Lord's work in a time of pressure, not about being a better Christian.

A widow in the Roman world was often under pressure to marry again, sometimes for money or family reasons, and Augustus's laws expected younger widows to remarry. Paul says she is free to marry ‘anyone she wishes’. In a world where families often arranged marriages for women, that is a striking freedom. His one limit is ‘as long as he belongs to the Lord’, that is, a fellow believer.

‘I think that I too have the Spirit of God’ may have a gentle edge. Some in Corinth claimed to be especially spiritual. Paul says, in effect, ‘So do I.’
passages.ot:
The Old Testament also saw marriage as binding for life. Paul uses the same picture in Romans: “a married woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of marriage” (Romans 7:2).

God is the defender of widows all through the Old Testament: “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5). Ruth, a widow, chose to stay with Naomi and with Naomi's God, and later married Boaz, a man of faith (Ruth 1 to 4).

Paul elsewhere advised younger widows to marry: “So I advise the younger widows to marry” (1 Timothy 5:14). That shows again that his advice here was for its time and its people, not a rule for every widow.
passages.asks: Paul leaves real choices in people's hands, and says both choices can be good. Ask whether you have been afraid of making the ‘wrong’ choice in an honest decision about marriage, work or where to live. Paul's words suggest that God is less anxious about it than you are. Ask what it would mean to choose freely, ‘in the Lord’.
